subject: moon-phases
title: Moon Phases: Geometry in the Sky
summary: Why phases are an angle, why the cycle runs 29.5 days, and why we see one face (mostly).

keys.answer: The changing Sun–observer–Moon angle: we see more or less of a Moon that is always half lit. Earth's shadow is not the cause.

keys.prompt: Why is the synodic month (about 29.5 days) longer than the 27.3-day orbit?
keys.answer: Earth advances along its orbit during the month, so the Moon must travel extra to line up with the Sun again.

keys.prompt: How did the Moon become tidally locked?
keys.answer: Earth's gravity tugged on a lagging tidal bulge; the flexing turned spin energy into heat until one spin matched one orbit.

cards.title: The missing lap
cards.text: The Moon goes around Earth about 13.4 times a year. Yet we see only about 12.4 cycles of phases. One whole lap seems to vanish every year. Where does it go?

cards.question: Tidal locking keeps one face toward Earth. Roughly what share of the Moon's surface has been imaged from the ground anyway?
cards.reveal: About 59%. Libration, an apparent wobble from the elliptical, tilted orbit, lets us peek around the edges.

cards.title: Phase is an angle, not a shadow
cards.text: The Sun always lights half the Moon. What changes is the elongation θ, the angle between the Moon and the Sun as seen from Earth. The lit fraction of the disk is (1 − cos θ)/2: 0 at new Moon, 50% at the quarters (90°, 270°), 100% at full (180°). Phases are the Moon's own night side turned partly toward us, not Earth's shadow.
cards.example: At θ = 60°, the lit fraction is (1 − 0.5)/2 = 25%: a crescent.

why.q: If Earth's shadow made the phases, what would we see that we don't?
why.a: Earth's shadow can only reach the Moon when it is opposite the Sun, at full Moon. That's a lunar eclipse, and the 5° tilt of the Moon's orbit means most full Moons miss the shadow.

cards.title: The lap that vanishes
cards.text: The Moon completes an orbit in about 27.3 days, but new Moon to new Moon averages 29.5. During the month Earth carries the system along its orbit, so the Moon must travel extra arc to line up with the Sun again. Over a year: 13.4 orbits, but only 12.4 passages between Earth and the Sun. The missing lap is Earth's own trip around the Sun.
cards.example: Hence calendars: 12 lunar months fall 10 or 11 days short of a solar year, so a purely lunar calendar like the Islamic Hijri calendar drifts through the seasons, while lunisolar calendars add a 13th month every few years.

cards.title: Phase sets the schedule
cards.text: Because phase is an angle from the Sun, it fixes rise and set times at most latitudes. A new Moon rises and sets with the Sun. First quarter rises around midday and sets around the middle of the night. Full rises at sunset and sets at sunrise. Third quarter rises around the middle of the night and sets around midday. A daytime Moon is common, not odd.
cards.example: Planning a moonlit night hike? A full Moon is up all night; a first quarter Moon sets around the middle of the night, leaving the back half dark.

cards.title: Tidal locking, then drift
cards.text: We see one face because the Moon spins once per orbit. NASA's account: Earth's gravity raised a bulge on the young, hot, closer Moon. As it spun, the bulge lagged and gravity kept tugging it back; the flexing turned spin energy into heat until one spin matched one orbit. The same exchange continues through Earth's oceans, slowing Earth's rotation and pushing the Moon away about 1.5 inches (4 cm) a year.

why.q: Why did the spin stop changing once it matched the orbit?
why.a: Once synchronized, the bulge no longer shifted relative to Earth, so there was no more flexing to dissipate energy and the spin rate stopped changing.

cards.title: Libration: seeing 59%
cards.text: The lock isn't perfect from our view. The orbit is elliptical, so the Moon's orbital speed varies while its spin stays constant: near its closest approach the spin falls behind and we see more of the eastern side; near its farthest the spin gets ahead and we see more of the western side. The 5° tilt of the orbit adds a north–south nod. Net result: around 59% of the surface has been imaged from the ground.

cards.question: Lunar months track something anyone can see; solar years track the seasons. If you were designing a calendar for a society, would you anchor it to the Moon, the Sun or both? What do you gain and lose with each?
nudges: Who most needs to know the season, and who most needs a sky anyone can read?
What does adding a 13th month every few years cost in simplicity?
Which choice would you defend if someone argued the other side?

questions.q: Using (1 − cos θ)/2, at what elongation is the Moon 75% lit?

options.why: At 90°, cos θ = 0, giving 50%: a quarter Moon.

questions.q: Why is the synodic month about two days longer than the Moon's 27.3-day orbit?

options.text: Earth moves along its orbit, so the Moon must go extra to line up with the Sun
options.why: Right. Phases are measured against the moving Earth–Sun line, not the stars.

options.text: The Moon slows down at full Moon
options.why: Orbital speed varies with distance, but that doesn't add two days on average.

options.text: Earth's shadow delays each new Moon
options.why: Earth's shadow plays no role in ordinary phases.

options.text: The 5° tilt of the Moon's orbit
options.why: The tilt explains why eclipses don't happen every month, not the month's length.

questions.q: You see a half-lit Moon rising around the middle of the night. Which phase is it?

options.why: Third quarter rises around the middle of the night and sets around midday.
First quarter rises around midday and sets around the middle of the night.
A waxing gibbous is more than half lit and rises in the afternoon.
A waning crescent is a thin sliver that rises in the very early morning.

sources.title: Moon Phases
sources.supports: Only the Sun shines with its own light; the Moon is always half-lit; first quarter means a quarter through the monthly journey and shows half of the lit half; the full Moon is technically the real half moon; at new Moon the lit side faces away from Earth; moonrise and moonset times for each phase; the 27.3-day orbit and 29.5-day cycle; libration from the elliptical orbit and the 5° orbital tilt; daytime moons.

sources.title: Lunar phase
sources.supports: Phases are not caused by Earth's shadow; the lit fraction is (1 − cos θ)/2 where θ is the elongation; 27.3-day orbit vs 29.5-day phase cycle because of Earth's orbit (13.4 orbits but 12.4 passages a year); eclipses need new or full Moon and the 5° tilt usually prevents them; around 59% of the surface imaged from the ground thanks to libration; 12 lunar months are 10 or 11 days short of a solar year, so lunar calendars drift and lunisolar calendars add a 13th month.

sources.title: Tidal Locking
sources.supports: The Moon spins once per orbit so the same side faces Earth; all the solar system's large moons are tidally locked; the lagging bulge, heat dissipation and slowing spin; the Moon drifts away about 1.5 inches (4 cm) a year, driven mainly by Earth's oceans, which also slows Earth's rotation.
